reps.md:
Vatra Dornei sits at about 800 m where the Dorna river meets the Golden Bistrița, in a mountain basin of south-west Bukovina. It is a small town of about 12,600 people with a big past. It was a customs post on the Moldavia–Transylvania road from the 1590s and a Habsburg town from 1775 to 1918, when it was called Dorna-Watra. In the late 19th century it became one of the empire's eastern spas, built on iron-rich carbonated water and peat mud.

Four layers sit on top of each other:
- **The Habsburg spa (1870s–1914).** The Church Fund of Bukovina owned the baths. Mayor Vasile Deac lobbied Vienna. The 1890s produced the Casino, the bath house, the spring pavilions, the Primăria, the electric plant (1895) and the railway (1902).
- **The multi-ethnic town.** Romanians, Jews (22% in 1930), Germans, Ruthenians and Poles. You can still read them in the buildings: a synagogue, an ex-Lutheran church, an ex-Greek-Catholic wooden church, a Catholic church.
- **War and catastrophe.** The WWI front on the Mestecăniș ridge (1916–17), shell tubes in the church wall, heroes' cemeteries. Then the 1941 deportation of the Jews from Gara Mare, and the retreating Germans' damage in 1944.
- **The socialist resource basin.** Manganese at Iacobeni and Ciocănești, sulphur in the Călimani volcano, the trade-union mass spa, the 1980 chairlift. Most of it closed in 1997.

Bearings: the spa core (Casino, park, Gara Băi) is on the south bank. Str. Mihai Eminescu runs west from the Primăria past the churches and the synagogue. Str. Negrești climbs to the chairlift. Gara Mare and the heroes' cemetery are north. The best sights for this map are in the basin, 10–60 km out: a car helps.

Everything here started with gas. Carbon dioxide rising from deep under the Călimani volcanic field dissolves into ordinary groundwater in the river terraces. That makes it acidic enough to take up iron, calcium and magnesium, and it comes out fizzing. The basin has dozens of such springs, called *borcut* or *borviz*. A customs officer found the town's iron spring in 1804. Naturalists analysed the waters from the 1780s on, and by 1857 Dorna's iron springs were ranked richer than Styria's Gleichenberg.

Follow the water as a chain. Sentinela and Unirea in town are the polite face. The Bradul mofettes are where you sit in dry CO₂. The F6 borehole at Dorna Candrenilor erupts. At Șaru Dornei, the "Carmen Sylva" water was bottled for a century and then shut in 1986 for arsenic. At Poiana Negrii, Coca-Cola now bottles "Dorna". At the Călimani sulphur quarry you see the volcanic plumbing exposed.

Start with: Sentinela, then Unirea spring, then Șaru Dornei on a day out.

The tourist guide sees a spa. The map sees a mining basin. In 1796 the Styrian Manz family bought the Iacobeni ironworks, brought German miners from Zips, and founded colonies and furnaces across the mountains. Their 1823 manor is still standing, derelict. After their 1859 bankruptcy the mines turned to manganese. Under socialism the basin supplied nearly all of Romania's manganese, and the state cut an open-pit sulphur mine into a volcano at 2,000 m, with a town for its workers and a villa for Ceaușescu. Almost all of it closed in 1997.

What you can see today: the 2.4 km² Arșița quarry; the Oița mine, where you can enter a gallery; the Călimani crater, its waste dumps and the Ceaușescu villa; and the Mestecăniș tunnels, one with a faked breakthrough. The town's own socialist fabric (block estates, mosaics) is still un-researched: look for it on arrival.

A lost one to keep in mind: Vatra Dornei had a bobsled track from the interwar years, run for decades and closed in 1955. Nobody online says where it was. If a local knows, it may have banked curves left in the forest.

Start with: Arșița and the Manz manor (half a day, Iacobeni), then Călimani in dry weather.

Dorna was a border town, and both world wars passed through it. In 1914–15 and again in 1916–17 the Russian army fought for the Carpathian passes here. Its artillery on the Mestecăniș ridge shelled the town: three duds hit the Catholic church, and their casings were set into its wall. Prisoners of war built military railways over the Prislop and Tihuța passes. Polish legionaries are buried at Cârlibaba, and a 24-year-old Tyrolean lies under a misspelled cross in the Catholic cemetery.

The second war ended the multi-ethnic town. The Germans were resettled in 1940. On 11 October 1941, about 2,650 Jews of the town and villages were put on two trains at Gara Mare and sent to Transnistria; many did not return. A plaque has marked the station and the synagogue since 2016. In 1944 the retreating Germans wrecked parts of the spa.

Read the monuments for their edits too. The 1936 heroes' obelisk lists 33 minority dead and lost its cross under communism. The spa park was given an avenue of national busts from 1964. The Sentinela spring was renamed "23 August".

Start with: Gara Mare, then the heroes' cemetery, then the Catholic church on Eminescu.

A spa sells stories. Sort them as you go:
- **Blaga lived at the Belvedere 1952–64.** Impossible. He died in 1961 and worked in Cluj. The villa was nationalised in 1948. The house did bear his name in the 1930s.
- **Famous guests at the Casino** (Iorga, Crainic, Beniuc…). Plausible, but no source has been traced.
- **Franz Joseph opened the Casino in person.** It appears in one newspaper story only. Unverified.
- **Stoker and the Borgo Pass.** Stoker never came. The "Dracula" hotel dates from 1976–83.
- **Dorina.** The town is said to be named after a shepherdess whom Prince Dragoș shot by mistake while hunting. This is legend, with no spot.
- **Megaliths at Gura Haitii.** A former raftsman's yard of carved river boulders, believed by him to be prehistoric sun symbols. A folk folly, not archaeology. Fun, though.
- **"Casa Ursu"** is just a modern guesthouse. There is no Armenian heritage site in town.

The real thinkers here are local historians. Paul Brașcanu dug out the shell casings, the Ziffer story and the Șaru Dornei springs. The Casa de Cultură still runs a monthly literary café.

No city pass. Prices change; these are from 2025–26 listings:
- **Casino:** Wed–Sun; official 11–18, Google says 12–16. About 20 lei (unconfirmed). Call 0744 422 733.
- **Ethnographic Museum** (Primăria): Tue–Sun 10–16, about 10 lei.
- **Natural Sciences Museum:** Tue–Fri 10–17, Sat–Sun 10–14, about 5 lei. Reopened September 2026.
- **Chairlift:** daily 10–16:30, 50 lei return. Weather and minimum riders apply.
- **Oița mine:** groups only, by appointment through the Țara Dornelor tourism office.
- **Ciocănești egg museum:** Mon–Fri 10–16, Sat 11–15, Sun 13–16.
- **Călimani visitor centre:** weekdays 10–14.
- **Dorna Candrenilor spa:** daily 10–21:30.

Late autumn: snow can close the Călimani quarry road and the Rarău road from November. Ski runs usually open only around New Year. Daylight is short, so do the basin in the mornings. Events: Christmas fair at the Casa de Cultură (about 15–23 Dec), village winter-custom shows on 24–27 Dec, the "Porniți plugul" mask festival on 28–29 Dec, and New Year's Eve on Str. Mihai Eminescu. The 2026 dates are not confirmed.

Getting around: two stations, Gara Mare (north) and Gara Băi (centre). Buses run to Suceava (about 2–2.5 h). For the basin you need a car or a local driver.
